title: Katzmann: Judicial interpretation as a practical inquiry (pp. 55–58, 90–91)
shortTitle: Katzmann: Judicial interpretation as a practical inquiry (pp. 55–58, 90–91)
summary: Katzmann describes a plural set of interpretive tools whose usefulness depends on the statutory question.
notes:
The reading lists text, structure, history, usage in related statutes, common law, agency interpretations, dictionaries, technical and everyday usage, canons, common practice, and purpose. Some provisions supply a straightforward answer; the examples of a quantitative pseudoephedrine limit and an obstruction statute illustrate why adding an unwritten requirement can be inappropriate. Specialized legal subjects and open-ended commands require different contextual work.

The three extended litigation sequences test the approach: Raila and Dolan concern statutory purpose and associated words, Gayle and Small the geographic reach of apparently broad language, and Murphy and Arlington the force of legislative history against text and a constitutional notice rule. Katzmann does not offer a mechanical hierarchy that guarantees agreement. He presents reasoned judgment oriented toward congressional meaning, while recognizing that appellate decisions are collective products and that his own interpretation can be reversed.
